## Abstract

In SGA 2, Grothendieck conjectures that the étale fundamental group of the punctured spectrum of a complete noetherian local domain of dimension at least two with algebraically closed residue field is topologically finitely generated. In this paper, we prove a weaker statement, namely that the maximal pro-nilpotent quotient of the fundamental group is topologically finitely generated. The proof uses p-adic nearby cycles and negative definiteness of intersection pairings over resolutions of singularities as well as some analysis of Lie algebras of certain algebraic group structures on deformation cohomology.

## Introduction

In SGA 2 [8], Grothendieck makes the following conjecture:

Conjecture 1.1 [8, Exposé XIII, Conjecture 3.1]

Let A be a complete noetherian local ring with algebraically closed residue field F and maximal ideal \mathfrak{m}. Let p be the characteristic of F if it is positive and let otherwise. Assume that the irreducible components of Spec A have dimension ≥2 and the scheme is connected. Then:

  * (1)

The étale fundamental group is topologically finitely generated.

  * (2)

The maximal pro-prime-to-p quotient of is topologically finitely presented.

This conjecture is in part based on Mumford's earlier study [15] in the complex-analytic setting, where a topological analogue of is shown to be finitely presented when the exceptional divisor of a resolution of singularities of A is simply connected (see [15, Section I, pp. 11–12]). Statement (2) is proved by Grothendieck-Murre [7, Theorem 9.2] when A is two-dimensional. Our focus in this paper is the pro-p part and hence Statement (1).

Grothendieck originally stated (1) in his letter to Serre dated October 1, 1961 [3], where Serre's editorial note (in 2000) reads: “I do not know whether any progress has been made on it since.” Known results indeed seem quite scarce: the only one the author could find (at the time this paper was submitted) is the work of Carvajal-Rojas-Schwede-Tucker [2], which proves that is finite of order prime to p for the case where A is a strongly F-regular singularity in equal characteristic . (But see below about the work of Hartshorne-Speiser [9].) On the other hand, wild quotient singularities constructed by Artin [1], Lorenzini [12, Corollary 6.14] and others give concrete examples with .

In this paper, we prove a weaker version of Statement (1) with no additional assumption on A:

Theorem 1.2

Under the assumptions of Conjecture 1.1, the maximal pro-nilpotent quotient of is topologically finitely generated.
It is enough to show that the maximal abelian quotient of is topologically finitely generated.^{1} The prime-to-p part is done by Grothendieck-Murre. Thus all we need to do is to show the finiteness of the étale cohomology

The strategy is to take a resolution of singularities of A and describe the {H}^{1} by p-adic nearby cycles around the exceptional divisor. These p-adic nearby cycles in turn are described by coherent cohomology. The negative definiteness of intersection matrices of exceptional divisors supplies basic bounds on the coherent cohomology. Additionally, we need to analyze a kind of Frobenius-fixed points of some “deformation” cohomology. This part is more involved in the mixed characteristic case than in the equal characteristic case. For this analysis, we introduce algebraic group structures on the deformation cohomology and use their Lie algebras.

When this paper was submitted, one of the referees pointed out that the equal characteristic case of Theorem 1.2 had essentially been obtained by Hartshorne-Speiser [9].

## 1. Statement of the main theorem and applications

Theorem 1.1.

Let \(S\) be a noetherian scheme, \(X\) and \(Y\) two proper \(S\)-schemes, \(f:X\longrightarrow Y\) a morphism. We assume \(S\) integral and \(f\) surjective. Then there exists a non-empty open \(V\) of \(S\) such that the morphism

\[f^*:\operatorname{Pic}_{Y/S}|V\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}_{X/S}|V\]

between the Picard functors (localized for the f.p.p.f topology) is representable by a quasi-affine morphism of finite presentation.

Corollary 1.2.

Let \(X\) be a proper scheme over a noetherian scheme \(S\). We assume \(S\) integral. Then there exists a non-empty open \(V\) of \(S\) such that the Picard functor \(\operatorname{Pic}_{X/S}|V\) is representable by a \(V\)-group scheme which is a sum of quasi-projective opens of finite type, hence a fortiori separated over \(V\).

Indeed, let us recall the following fact (FGA N°232): let \(S\) be a scheme, \(X\) a projective \(S\)-scheme, of finite presentation and integral over \(S\) (that is to say flat with geometrically integral fibres). 
Finally, 1.1 says that after possibly shrinking \(V\) and \(S'\), the morphism \(f^*:\operatorname{Pic}_{X'/S'}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}_{Z'/S'}\) is representable by a quasi-affine morphism. Consequently \(\operatorname{Pic}_{X'/S'}\) is representable by a group scheme, a sum of quasi-projective open subschemes of finite type; thanks to finite flat descent (SGA 1 VIII 7.6 and EGA II 6.6.1), so is \(\operatorname{Pic}_{X/S}|V\).

Lemma 1.4.

Let \(k\) be a field, \(P\) and \(Q\) two \(k\)-group schemes locally of finite type and let \(f:P\longrightarrow Q\) be a quasi-affine morphism. Then \(f\) is affine.

Indeed let \(R=\operatorname{Ker}(f)\); \(R\) is a \(k\)-group scheme of finite type which is quasi-affine; by virtue of (SGA 3 VI_{B} 11.11), \(R\) is then affine.

Therefore \(P\longrightarrow P/R\), which makes \(P\) a \(R\)-torsor over \(P/R\), is affine. Moreover it is known (SGA 3 1.4.2) that \(P/R\longrightarrow Q\) is a closed immersion, hence affine, hence the same holds for the composite \(P\longrightarrow P/R\longrightarrow Q\).

Corollary 1.5.

Let \(k\) be a field.

a) Let \(X\) be a proper \(k\)-scheme. Then \(\operatorname{Pic}_{X/k}\) is representable (J.P. Murre).

b) Let \(f:X\longrightarrow Y\) be a surjective morphism between two proper \(k\)-schemes. Then the induced morphism \(f^*:\operatorname{Pic}_{Y/k}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}_{X/k}\) is affine.

Corollary 1.6.

Let \(S\) be an integral noetherian scheme, \(f:X\longrightarrow Y\) a surjective \(S\)-morphism between two proper \(S\)-schemes.

a) If \(Y\) is normal over \(S\) (that is, flat with geometrically normal fibres), then, after possibly shrinking \(S\), \(f^*:\operatorname{Pic}_{Y/S}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}_{X/S}\) is quasi-finite.

b) If \(\operatorname{Pic}_{Y/S}\) is essentially proper over \(S\) (that is, if it satisfies the valuative criterion of properness, for example, if \(Y\) is smooth over \(S\)) then after possibly shrinking \(S\), \(f^*:\operatorname{Pic}_{Y/S}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}_{X/S}\) is finite (and in particular, affine).

Indeed in a), for every \(s\in S\), \(R_s=\operatorname{Ker}(f_s^*)\) is an affine algebraic group; its identity component is an algebraic group proper over \(k\) (FGA 236, Théorème 2.1 (iii)); \(R_s\) is therefore finite. In b) \(f^*\) is both proper and quasi-affine, hence finite.

Remark 1.7.

It is not known whether 1.1 remains valid when "quasi-affine" is replaced by affine, as 1.5 and 1.6 might suggest.

Proof. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be an invertible $\mathcal{O}_ U$-module with pullback $\mathcal{L}^\wedge $ on $U^\wedge $. We have $H^0(U, \mathcal{O}_ U) = A$ by our assumption on depth and Dualizing Complexes, Lemma 47.11.1 and Local Cohomology, Lemma 51.8.2. Thus $\mathcal{L}$ is trivial if and only if $M = H^0(U, \mathcal{L})$ is isomorphic to $A$ as an $A$-module. (Details omitted.) Since $A \to A^\wedge $ is flat we have $M \otimes _ A A^\wedge = \Gamma (U^\wedge , \mathcal{L}^\wedge )$ by flat base change, see Cohomology of Schemes, Lemma 30.5.2. Finally, it is easy to see that $M \cong A$ if and only if $M \otimes _ A A^\wedge \cong A^\wedge $. $\square$

Lemma 52.27.5. Let $(A, \mathfrak m)$ be a regular local ring. Then the Picard group of the punctured spectrum of $A$ is trivial.

Proof. Combine Divisors, Lemma 31.29.3 with More on Algebra, Lemma 15.123.2. $\square$

Now we can bootstrap the earlier results to prove that Picard groups are trivial for punctured spectra of complete intersections of dimension $\geq 4$. Recall that a Noetherian local ring is called a complete intersection if its completion is the quotient of a regular local ring by the ideal generated by a regular sequence. See the discussion in Divided Power Algebra, Section 23.8.

Proposition 52.27.6 (Grothendieck). Let $(A, \mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian local ring. If $A$ is a complete intersection of dimension $\geq 4$, then the Picard group of the punctured spectrum of $A$ is trivial.

Proof. By Lemma 52.27.4 we may assume that $A$ is a complete local ring. By assumption we can write $A = B/(f_1, \ldots , f_ r)$ where $B$ is a complete regular local ring and $f_1, \ldots , f_ r$ is a regular sequence. We will finish the proof by induction on $r$. The base case is $r = 0$ which follows from Lemma 52.27.5.

## 9 The strict logarithmic Jacobian and the Picard space

Over a Dedekind base S, Raynaud constructed the Néron model of the Jacobian of a curve X / S as the quotient of the relative Picard space by the closure e ¯ of the unit section (see [5, Section 9.5]). When dim ⁡ S > 1 , the closure e ¯ is in general neither S-flat nor a subgroup, and so this quotient is not representable. In [12] and [31], necessary and sufficient conditions for the flatness of e ¯ are given, proving the existence of separated Néron models when these conditions hold. In this section we show that Raynaud’s approach can be extended over higher-dimensional bases even when e ¯ is not S-flat, simply by replacing e ¯ by its largest open subspace e ¯ e ´ ⁢ t which is étale over S. This allows us to describe the Néron model (constructed above as the algebraic space sLPic 0 ) as the quotient of the Picard space by e ¯ e ´ ⁢ t , under somewhat more restrictive assumptions on X / S . The construction of the Néron model in [33] is done by gluing local models of this form.

Letting π : X → S be a log curve, we write Pic tot0 for the kernel of the composition

Pic X / S → ℤ ⁢ [ Irr X / S ] → Σ ℤ .

There is a canonical map Pic X / S tot0 → sLPic X / S 0 taking a line bundle to the associated log line bundle.

Write e ¯ for the schematic closure of the unit section in Pic X / S tot0 . If U, V ↪ e ¯ are open immersions étale over S, then the same is true of their union. Hence e ¯ has a largest open subscheme which is étale over S, which we denote by e ¯ e ´ ⁢ t , a locally closed subscheme of Pic X / S tot0 .

## Theorem 9.1.

Suppose that S is log regular. Then:

  1. The map f : Pic X / S tot0 → sLPic X / S 0 has kernel e ¯ e ´ ⁢ t .

  2. If in addition X ¯ is regular, then f is surjective.
